chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Isḥaq ibn ʿAmmār, who said:

I said to Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): 'For the absent husband who divorces his wife, what is her waiting period (ghaybah)?' He said, 'Five months, six months.' I said, 'A limit less than that?' He said, 'Three months.'

So there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first report we mentioned earlier, because the method of reconciling them is that the ruling varies according to the variation of women's customs regarding menstruation. So whoever knows of his wife's condition that she menstruates every month, it is permissible for him to divorce her after the month ends. And whoever knows that she does not menstruate except every three months, it is not permissible for him to divorce her except after the three months end. And likewise for the one who menstruates every six months, and there is no contradiction between them in any way.
ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for a woman whose husband is absent and she seeks divorce?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the ʿiddah for a woman with an irregular or unknown menstrual cycle is determined by her specific habitual cycle (ʿādah), ranging from three to six months. This ruling resolves apparent contradictions in earlier texts by linking the legal duration to the physiological reality of the individual, reflecting the Shia scholarly principle of adapting fixed rulings to variable natural conditions.
